related-article.article-title: Study of brentuximab vedotin combination treatment in people with early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma: a plain language summary

list-item.p: AN+AD resulted in an objective response rate of 96%, CR rate of 92%, and 2-year progression-free survival of 97%.
Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events in 44%; grade ≥3 treatment-related peripheral sensory neuropathy in 3%; no febrile neutropenia.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Most patients with early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) are treated with doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine with or without radiation therapy, although studies are now evaluating the incorporation of novel agents paired with abbreviated chemotherapy. We present the efficacy and safety of AN+AD (brentuximab vedotin [BV] and nivolumab in combination with doxorubicin and dacarbazine) in patients with early-stage cHL. In this phase 2 study, patients with nonbulky (<10 cm) Ann Arbor stage I or II cHL received 4 cycles of AN+AD. The primary end point was complete response (CR) rate at end of treatment (EOT) by investigator. At the time of this analysis, 154 patients received ≥1 dose of AN+AD. The objective response rate at EOT was 96% (95% confidence interval [CI], 91.7-98.6), and the CR rate was 92% (95% CI, 86.0-95.4). In the favorable (n = 56) and unfavorable (n = 97) subgroups, CR rates were 95% (95% CI, 85.1-98.9) and 91% (95% CI, 83.1-95.7), respectively. The proportion of patients with duration of CR of at least 2 years was 96% (95% CI, 90.9-98.4). At a median follow-up of 27.9 months, the estimated 2-year progression-free survival rate was 97% (95% CI, 92.0-98.8). Any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 99% and 44% of patients, respectively; no events of febrile neutropenia were reported. Any-grade treatment-emergent immune-mediated adverse events occurred in 22% of patients. One disease-related death was reported after the safety reporting period. Results from this study support the use of BV and nivolumab in combination with limited chemotherapy for patients with nonbulky, early-stage cHL. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03646123.

Most patients with early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) are treated with chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy. Abramson and colleagues report the efficacy and safety of the anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin (BV) and the anti-PD1 antibody nivolumab in combination with doxorubicin and dacarbazine chemotherapy (AN+AD) for the treatment of nonbulky cHL in 154 patients. Four cycles of AN+AD achieve a complete response rate of 92% (95% confidence interval [CI], 86.0%-95.4%) and an estimated 2-year progression-free survival rate of 97% (95% CI, 92.0%-98.8%). These encouraging data support the use of BV and nivolumab in regimens for patients with early-stage cHL.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) resulted in 82 409 new cases and 22 701 deaths globally in 2022.1 Approximately 95% of HL cases are classical HL (cHL), whereas the remainder represent nodular lymphocyte predominant HL.2 In 2024, an estimated 8570 new cases of cHL were diagnosed in the United States.3 cHL is diagnosed based on the presence of malignant Reed-Sternberg cells.2 These cells express CD30 and overexpress programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1).4 Patients with early-stage cHL have historically been treated with combined-modality strategies using combination chemotherapy followed by involved-site radiation therapy (ISRT) in most cases.2 However, to improve clinical outcomes, reduce chemotherapy use, and eliminate the need for radiation therapy, novel agents are being incorporated into treatment regimens.5, 6, 7

Brentuximab vedotin (BV) is an antibody-drug conjugate composed of an anti-CD30 monoclonal antibody conjugated by a protease-cleavable linker to the microtubule-disrupting agent, monomethyl auristatin E, allowing for targeted delivery of the monomethyl auristatin E payload into CD30-expressing cells. In addition to direct cytotoxicity, some molecular studies have proposed other mechanisms of action leading to cellular disruption.8, 9, 10, 11 Based on the phase 3 ECHELON-1 trial, A+AVD (BV in combination with doxorubicin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine) is approved as a frontline standard-of-care option for patients with advanced cHL and has demonstrated an overall survival (OS) benefit.12 Although A+AVD improved efficacy outcomes compared with ABVD (combination of doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine), rates of peripheral neuropathy (67%) and febrile neutropenia (19%) were higher with A+AVD.12,13 More recently, BrECADD (BV in combination with etoposide, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, dacarbazine, and dexamethasone) has been approved for stage IIB to IV cHL in the European Union based on the results of the phase 3 HD21 trial.7,14

Toxicity associated with A+AVD likely results from the overlapping mechanisms of action of BV and vinblastine, which are both microtubule disrupters and can cause neuropathy and myelosuppression.15 In patients with nonbulky early-stage cHL, A+AVD resulted in a high complete response (CR) rate but toxicities were high.15 A subsequent phase 2 study of BV plus doxorubicin and dacarbazine in nonbulky early-stage cHL demonstrated the ability to omit vinblastine and radiation, with a very high CR rate of 97% and a 5-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate of 91%. Through the omission of vinblastine, the incidence of peripheral sensory neuropathy decreased, with most events being grade 1 and none being grade ≥3. Furthermore, febrile neutropenia did not occur despite a lack of prophylactic granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) use.16

Nivolumab is a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)–blocking antibody with strong activity in relapsed or refractory cHL and demonstrated efficacy in frontline therapy in combination with AVD.17,18 In a phase 1/2 study, the combination of BV and nivolumab showed durable efficacy without additional toxicity concerns in this patient population.19,20 Another phase 2 study showed promising durable efficacy of this doublet as frontline treatment in older patients with cHL,21 indicating potential benefit in early-stage cHL.18 PD-1 blockade in combination with BV has been shown to enhance antitumor immunity by depleting T regulatory cells, inducing inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, and enhancing antigen-specific T-cell response.11,19,20

Overall, these studies provide the rationale to investigate the novel combination of AN+AD (BV, nivolumab, doxorubicin, and dacarbazine), while omitting bleomycin, vinblastine, and radiation, among patients with both early-stage and advanced-stage cHL. The phase 2 SGN35-027 study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03646123) is a multipart clinical trial of BV in cHL. Part B of this study assessed AN+AD in patients with advanced-stage cHL and showed efficacy comparable to other regimens and a favorable safety profile.22 Here, we present the efficacy and safety of AN+AD from the part C portion of this study for patients with early-stage cHL.

sec.title: Trial participants
sec.p: Eligible patients were aged ≥12 years in the United States and aged ≥18 years outside the United States with treatment-naive histologically confirmed Ann Arbor stage I or II cHL without bulky mediastinal disease (<10 cm in diameter on computed tomography [CT]). Patients had bidimensional measurable disease (as documented by positron emission tomography [PET]/CT or CT imaging) and ≥1 lesion measuring >1.5 cm in the longest diameter on cross-sectional imaging, measurable in 2 perpendicular dimensions on CT (or magnetic resonance imaging), and fluorodeoxyglucose avid on PET. Patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 to 2. German Hodgkin Study Group (GHSG) risk criteria were used to define favorable and unfavorable disease at diagnosis.23,24 Patients were excluded if they fulfilled any of the following criteria: nodular lymphocyte predominant HL; active cerebral/meningeal disease related to underlying malignancy, including signs or symptoms of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; a history of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, therapeutic radiation, or any immunotherapy within 4 weeks of the first study drug dose; or prior treatment with an anti–PD-1, anti–PD-L1, anti–PD-L2, or anti–CTLA-4 antibody.

sec.title: Study design and treatment
sec.p: Patients received 4 cycles of treatment with 1.2 mg/kg of BV, capped at a maximum body weight of 100 kg; 240 mg of nivolumab; 25 mg/m2 of doxorubicin; and 375 mg/m2 of dacarbazine. All study drugs were administered separately by intravenous infusion on days 1 and 15 of each 28-day cycle. Study drugs were administered in the following order: doxorubicin and dacarbazine, followed by BV and then nivolumab. Nivolumab was administered ≥30 minutes after the end of the BV infusion. Similar to the phase 2 study with BV plus doxorubicin and dacarbazine,16 G-CSF was optional in this study because the incidence of febrile neutropenia was expected to be low. Patients were allowed premedications consistent with standard institutional practice, including antiemesis and the prevention of infusion-related reactions, including corticosteroids (<10 mg/d prednisone equivalent or per local standard of care). Immunosuppressive doses of systemic corticosteroids (>10 mg/d prednisone) were not allowed.

sec.title: Trial oversight
sec.p: This study was designed by the sponsors in collaboration with an advisory committee. The trial received approval from the independent site institutional review boards or ethics committees and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines defined by the International Council for Harmonization. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: End points
sec.p: The primary end point was the CR rate at the end of treatment (EOT). Secondary end points included safety and tolerability, objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), duration of CR (DOCR), event-free survival, PFS, and OS.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Staging was performed using CT scans of diagnostic quality and PET scans at baseline, during days 25 to 28 of cycle 2 (interim PET-2), at EOT, and during long-term follow-up. Disease involvement was determined by focal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in nodal and visceral sites that was consistent with lymphoma. PET scan metabolic uptake was graded using the Deauville 5-point scale, with a score of ≤3 considered a complete metabolic response.25 Patients in long-term follow-up did not need to undergo PET if the prior PET result was negative; instead, imaging assessments were conducted with CT. All imaging assessments were performed by the investigators. Safety evaluations included surveillance and recording of adverse events (AEs, including serious AEs), concomitant medications, physical examination results, and laboratory test results. Investigator-assessed AEs were graded per the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.03. Disease response and progression were assessed by the investigator using the Lugano classification revised staging system for malignant lymphoma,26 incorporating Lymphoma Response to Immunomodulatory Therapy Criteria for nodal non-HL and HL.27

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: A sample size of 150 was targeted to provide an adequate level of precision to reject the null hypothesis that the CR rate at EOT would be ≤90%. Assuming a CR rate of 95%, 150 patients would provide ∼80% power to reject the null hypothesis with a 1-sided α of 0.05 and using an empirical variance estimate.

ORRs, defined as the proportion of patients with a CR or partial response at EOT, and exact 2-sided 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using the Clopper-Pearson method were calculated. DOR was defined as the time from the first documentation of objective tumor response to the first documentation of progressive disease (PD) or death, whichever came first. DOCR was defined as the time from the first documentation of CR to the first documentation of PD or death, whichever came first. PFS was defined as the time from the start of study treatment to the first documentation of objective PD or death. Patients without progression or death were censored on the date of the last radiological assessment. DOR, DOCR, and PFS were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method. DOR, DOCR, and PFS rates and the associated 95% CIs were calculated using complementary log-log transformation.28

sec.title: Patient disposition and baseline characteristics
sec.p:
Overall, 156 patients were enrolled; 154 received ≥1 dose of the study drug. At the data cutoff of 4 October 2024, all patients were off study treatment; 147 patients (94%) completed treatment, 4 (3%) discontinued due to AEs, 2 (1%) discontinued due to patient decision, and 1 (1%) discontinued due to investigator decision. Median age was 31 years (range, 18-77), 16% were aged ≥60 years, 55% were female, 84% were White individuals, 89% had stage II disease, 11% had extranodal disease, 23% had B symptoms present at diagnosis, and 63% had unfavorable disease per GHSG risk criteria at diagnosis (Table 1). Median relative dose intensity of BV was 97.4% (range, 65%-104%).Table 1.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p:
At the time of this analysis, the ORR at EOT was 96% (95% CI, 91.7-98.6; n = 148/154) and the CR rate was 92% (95% CI, 86.0-95.4; n = 141/154; Table 2). In the favorable and unfavorable subgroups, CR rates were 95% (95% CI, 85.1-98.9; n = 53/56) and 91% (95% CI, 83.1-95.7; n = 88/97), respectively. Of the 3 indeterminate responses at EOT, 2 patients had a best overall response of CR and 1 had a partial response without subsequent progression. The estimated 2-year DOR rate was 96%. The proportion of patients with a duration of CR of at least 2 years was 96% (95% CI, 90.9-98.4).Table 2.

At a median follow-up of 27.9 months (95% CI, 27.2-28.6) for PFS, the estimated PFS rate at 2 years was 97% (95% CI, 92.0-98.8; Figure 1). No PD events were reported in patients who had favorable disease at diagnosis. Five patients had PD, all of whom had unfavorable disease at diagnosis; 2-year PFS rate was 95% (supplemental Figure 1, available on the Blood website). The estimated 2-year PFS rate was 98% in patients who had an EOT Deauville score (DS) of 1 or 2 (n = 98) and 97% in those who had an EOT DS of 3 (n = 34; supplemental Figure 2). At a median follow-up of 30.9 months for OS, only 1 event was reported. This event occurred in a 62-year-old woman with stage II unfavorable disease who died due to a second primary malignancy (mantle cell lymphoma) in long-term follow-up, 215 days after any study treatment.Figure 1.

At the time of interim PET-2, the ORR was 100% (95% CI, 97.6-100; n = 154/154) and the CR rate was 88% (95% CI, 82.2-92.9; n = 136/154; Table 2); 136 patients were PET-negative (DS, 1-3) and 17 were PET-positive (DS, 4 or 5; supplemental Table 1). At EOT, among the interim PET-2–negative patients, 124 (91%) were PET-negative and 9 (7%) were PET-positive. Among the interim PET-2–positive patients, 7 (41%) were PET-negative and 10 (59%) were PET-positive. The estimated 2-year PFS rate was 97% among patients who had an interim DS of 1 or 2 (n = 89), 98% in those with a DS of 3 (n = 47), 92% in those with a DS of 4 (n = 13), and 100% in those with a DS of 5 (n = 4; supplemental Figure 3).

Most patients (98%) received 4 cycles of treatment (Table 3). Subsequent cancer therapy for cHL was given to 5 patients (3%) at the discretion of the treating investigator; 2 received consolidative radiotherapy at the discretion of the treating investigator (both while in CR), 2 received systemic therapy for relapsed disease, and 1 received systemic therapy for PD. Patients who received consolidative radiotherapy were in CR at the time of consolidation. Sixty-seven patients (44%) received G-CSF during treatment, most of which (63/67 [94%]) was given as primary prophylaxis although G-CSF was not required per protocol. Patients who were administered G-CSF as a primary/secondary prophylaxis received it for a median of 2 days, and 39 patients (25%) received 4 cycles of G-CSF for primary prophylaxis (supplemental Table 2).Table 3.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
Any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) occurred in 153 (99%) and 67 patients (44%), respectively. No febrile neutropenia was reported. Any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) occurred in 149 (97%) and 52 patients (34%; Table 4). The most common (occurring in >20% of patients) any-grade TRAEs were nausea (65%), peripheral sensory neuropathy (47%), fatigue (44%), constipation (29%), and alopecia (22%); the most common (occurring in ≥5% of patients) grade ≥3 TRAEs were neutropenia (9%), alanine aminotransferase increase (6%), and aspartate aminotransferase increase (5%). Any-grade treatment-related pneumonitis occurred in 3 patients (2%), of whom 2 (1%) had grade ≥3 pneumonitis; the onset of treatment-related pneumonitis was between cycle 2 day 15 and cycle 312. Of 87 patients (56%) who experienced peripheral neuropathy, 52 (60%) had ongoing events at the last follow-up (grade 1 in 43 and grade 2 in 9; Table 5). Among all 106 recorded peripheral neuropathy events (patients may have experienced >1 event), 50 (47%) events resolved, 5 (5%) improved, and 51 (48%) neither improved nor resolved at the time of data cutoff. One death due to a second primary malignancy was reported after the safety reporting period.Table 4.

Serious TEAEs occurred in 29 patients (19%). Serious TRAEs occurred in 19 patients (12%), with the most common being pyrexia (3%). TEAEs led to discontinuation of all study drugs in 15 patients (10%), most commonly due to alanine aminotransferase increase (3%) and pneumonitis (1%). TEAEs led to discontinuation of BV in 4 patients (3%) due to drug-induced liver injury, peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, peripheral sensory neuropathy, or pneumonitis (1 event each). TEAEs led to discontinuation of nivolumab in 13 patients (8%), doxorubicin in 1 (1%), and dacarbazine in 1 (1%).

Any-grade treatment-emergent immune-mediated AEs (IMAEs) with a potential immunologic cause occurred in 34 patients (22%), most commonly hypothyroidism (6%), hyperthyroidism (5%), and maculopapular rash (4%; Table 6). Grade ≥3 IMAEs occurred in 12 patients (8%). IMAEs led to discontinuation of nivolumab in 5 patients (3%), due to pneumonitis in 2 patients (1%), alanine aminotransferase increase in 1 (1%), hepatitis in 1 (1%), and thyroiditis in 1 (1%). Patients received concomitant medications for a median duration of 15 days (range, 3-88) to treat IMAEs. Of the 34 patients with IMAEs, 12 patients (35%) had resolution of all IMAEs (supplemental Table 3). Among the 44 IMAE events, 20 (45%) events resolved with a median time to resolution of 5.1 weeks.Table 6.

In patients aged ≥60 years, pneumonitis occurred in 2 patients (1 with grade 2 and 1 with grade 3 event). The grade 3 event was considered serious. Both patients permanently discontinued nivolumab, and the patient with the grade 2 event also permanently discontinued BV. There was 1 event of suspected pneumonitis due to IMAE, which was later determined to be Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia based on polymerase chain reaction results.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Nonbulky early-stage cHL is a highly curable disease, but the combined-modality strategy is associated with short- and long-term risks.2 Data from the past investigator-initiated study of BV plus doxorubicin and dacarbazine highlighted the success of this regimen in decreasing peripheral sensory neuropathy with the omission of vinblastine, as well as the absence of febrile neutropenia, and served as the foundation for this AN+AD study.16 The results of this study demonstrate the efficacy of the AN+AD regimen for patients with early-stage cHL, as evidenced by the CR rate of 92% at EOT, 96% of responders with a DOR of 2 years, and the 2-year PFS rate of 97%. In addition, the safety profile of the regimen is notable for the absence of febrile neutropenia and the low risk of peripheral sensory neuropathy, liver toxicity, and IMAEs.

Efficacy results from this study are consistent with those of the current standard-of-care regimens for early-stage cHL, with the safety advantage of omitting bleomycin, vinblastine, and ISRT. In patients who had favorable disease at diagnosis, no PD events were reported with AN+AD at 2 years. In the phase 3 GHSG HD16 study of patients with favorable early-stage cHL, the 5-year PFS rate was 94.2% with the combined-modality treatment of 2 cycles of ABVD and 20 Gy of involved-field radiotherapy (IFRT) or PET-guided treatment and was 86.7% in patients treated with 2 cycles of ABVD who achieved CR (DS, 1 and 2 only) based on PET scan and did not go on to receive radiation therapy.29 Similar results were observed in the phase 3 RAPID PET-adapted study in early-stage cHL, with a 3-year PFS rate of 94.6% with combined-modality treatment and 90.8% with no additional therapy after 3 cycles of ABVD (DS, 1 and 2 only).30

Importantly, patients with early unfavorable disease also did extremely well on our study, with a 2-year PFS rate of 95%. In the RATHL study, the 3-year PFS rate was 90.0% in patients who had stage II disease and were treated with 6 cycles of ABVD/AVD.31 A total of 42% of patients in this study had stage II disease. In the phase 2 CALGB 50604 study of patients with early-stage cHL, 2- and 3-year PFS rates were 93% and 91%, respectively, after 2 cycles of ABVD without radiation when CR was shown by PET scan, to complete a total of 4 cycles of ABVD.32 In this study, 60% of patients had unfavorable and 40% had favorable disease per the GHSG criteria.

Parallel studies have also evaluated the incorporation of novel agents to treat patients with unfavorable cHL. A Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center–sponsored phase 2 study of unfavorable early-stage cHL found a 2-year PFS rate of 94% with 4 cycles of A+AVD without radiotherapy, supporting the elimination of consolidative radiation in patients with negative PET scan after 4 cycles of treatment.33 In the phase 2 BREACH study, the 2-year PFS rate was 97.3% with 4 cycles of A+AVD, G-CSF, and 30 Gy of ISRT in patients with unfavorable cHL per the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Lymphoma Study Association criteria.6 In the phase 2 GHSG NIVAHL study in early-stage unfavorable cHL, nivolumab + AVD resulted in a 1-year PFS rate of 100% with concomitant treatment and 98% with sequential treatment.5 The GHSG HD21 study of BrECADD included patients with stage II disease with B symptoms and large mediastinal mass and/or extranodal lesions as well as stage III/IV cHL. In the HD21 study, the 4-year PFS rate was 96.5% in patients with stage II disease.7

The aforementioned RAPID study established the use of PET avidity as a biomarker for treatment selection among patients with nonbulky cHL.30 In this study, patients received 3 cycles of ABVD and then underwent PET. Patients who were PET-positive (DS of 3-5) received an additional cycle of ABVD and IFRT, whereas those who were PET-negative (DS of 1 or 2) were randomly assigned to receive either IFRT or no further treatment. A follow-up analysis showed that patients with an interim PET-2 DS of 5 had inferior outcomes, whereas patients with a PET DS of 3 or 4 after 3 cycles of ABVD were treated effectively with a fourth cycle of ABVD and IFRT.34 Similarly, the CALGB 50604 study reinforced the predictive value of interim PET; the estimated 3-year PFS rate was 94% in patients with a DS of 1 or 2, 77% in those with a score of 3, and 67% in those with a score of 4 or 5.32 These results further confirm the excellent PFS with limited chemotherapy and omission of radiation therapy in most patients with early-stage nonbulky cHL using interim PET/CT as an indicator of response, thereby reducing the risks of radiation therapy. The phase 3 H10 trial of patients with stage I or II disease also evaluated a PET-adapted approach after 2 cycles of ABVD. The 5-year PFS rates were 89.6% and 92.1% in patients with unfavorable PET-negative disease treated with either 4 additional cycles of ABVD alone or 2 cycles of ABVD followed by involved-node radiotherapy, respectively; 18.8% of patients had PET-positive disease, with 5-year PFS rates of 77.4% and 90.6% in patients treated with 2 cycles of ABVD or 2 cycles of eBEACOPP (combination of bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone) followed by involved-node radiotherapy, respectively.35

Notably, in our study, the estimated 2-year PFS rates were similar across patients with an interim PET-2 DS of 1 to 5, ranging from 92% to 100%, consistent with the overall 2-year PFS rate of 97%. The consistent efficacy across patients with different DSs highlights the efficacy of AN+AD independent of interim PET-2 results. However, the small sample size (n = 4) of patients with a DS of 5 may not accurately reflect the PFS rates in this patient population. It is possible that interim PET may not be as reliable of a biomarker in the setting of nivolumab-containing chemotherapy due to inflammatory uptake observed in the setting of immune checkpoint inhibition.

In this study, the safety profile of AN+AD was notable for the absence of febrile neutropenia and bleomycin-related lung toxicity, but toxicities known to occur with BV (eg, peripheral neuropathy) and nivolumab (eg, IMAEs) were present, although manageable. Any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-related peripheral sensory neuropathy occurred in 47% and 3% of patients, respectively. These results can be compared with those of a phase 2 trial of patients with early-stage disease treated with 4 to 6 cycles of A+AVD, in which any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-related peripheral sensory neuropathy occurred in 79% and 24% of patients, respectively.15 The lower rates of peripheral neuropathy with AN+AD suggest that the omission of vinblastine significantly reduces peripheral neuropathy. Furthermore, with follow-up after the completion of AN+AD, most peripheral neuropathy events had either resolved or improved. One limitation of this study was that the doses of steroids were not recorded. However, steroids were not recommended as primary prophylaxis for IMAEs, and the incidence of such events was low. Further clarity on the medical management of IMAEs would be of interest in future studies.

The addition of nivolumab was associated with some IMAEs. Any-grade treatment-emergent IMAEs occurred in 22% of patients; however, the rate of nivolumab discontinuation was low (3%). IMAEs reported in this study with first-line AN+AD were consistent with the safety profile of nivolumab alone36 and those in patients with relapsed or refractory cHL treated with BV plus nivolumab.19

Given that false-positive PET results have been observed in studies after treatment with checkpoint inhibitors, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has the potential to provide a more precise measurement of tumor burden.37 A pilot study suggested that ctDNA changes during treatment might have predictive value and complement PET/CT assessments.38 Additional analyses are ongoing.39

Several trials assessing BV and/or nivolumab in combination with chemotherapy regimens in early-stage cHL are currently in progress. The phase 3 RADAR study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04685616) is recruiting eligible patients with previously untreated stage IA/IIA cHL who will be randomized to receive either ABVD or BV+AVD. The study has a PET response–adapted design that introduces BV into the treatment schema, similar to the regimen evaluated previously in RAPID. AHOD2131 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05675410), led by a National Cancer Institute cooperative group, is a randomized, multiarm, phase 3 trial enrolling both children and adults with newly diagnosed, previously untreated stage I and II cHL investigating the addition of BV with nivolumab after abbreviated chemotherapy vs standard treatment (chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy) using an interim PET–adapted approach.40 The phase 2 RAFTING study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04866654) is assessing radiation-free therapy, which will include nivolumab consolidation in high-burden, limited-stage cHL. Bleomycin is still included for all patients in this study, whereas the complete omission of bleomycin for all patients was a goal of our study.

In conclusion, these results from part C of the SGN35-027 study show that BV and nivolumab without bleomycin and vinblastine (AN+AD) in nonbulky early-stage disease has excellent efficacy and safety outcomes and facilitates the omission of consolidative ISRT. The CR rate was 92% and the 24-month PFS rate was 97%, and PFS rates were independent of interim PET-2 or baseline risk status. Furthermore, no febrile neutropenia occurred, and peripheral sensory neuropathy was low grade given vinblastine omission. These results also provide support for the continued evaluation of the BV plus nivolumab doublet in the ongoing AHOD 2131 trial. Future trials evaluating the AN+AD regimen in early-stage cHL can be considered. Both the high excellent CR rate and durable PFS highlight the ability of this AN+AD regimen to decrease toxicity related to traditional chemotherapy drugs given by eliminating bleomycin and vinblastine. The use of ctDNA to guide number of cycles and treatment intensity should be considered in future studies.
